title: Thinking in Probabilities
subtitle: Almost nothing in life is certain, yet our minds crave yes-or-no answers. Learning to think in odds instead of certainties is the first upgrade to how you reason.
hook: Ask most people "will it rain tomorrow?" and they want a yes or no. But the honest answer is a *number* — a 30% chance, say. The world runs on uncertainty, and the single most useful mental upgrade you can make is to stop demanding certainty and start thinking in **probabilities**. This is lesson one of the Ideas & Minds track, and it's the foundation for everything that follows: updating beliefs with evidence, weighing decisions, and spotting where your gut lies to you.

sections.heading: Probability is just a proportion
sections.body:
A probability is a number from **0 (impossible)** to **1 (certain)** — often written as a percentage — measuring how likely something is. The cleanest way to picture it: out of all the ways things could turn out, what *fraction* are the outcome you care about?

Roll a fair die. There are 6 equally likely outcomes. Rolling a 4 is **1 out of 6 ≈ 0.17 (17%)**. Rolling an even number is **3 out of 6 = 0.5 (50%)**. That's the whole core idea: favorable outcomes ÷ total possible outcomes, when each is equally likely.

sections.caption: Probability as a slice of all possible outcomes. The 'sample space' is everything that could happen; the event is the part you care about.

sections.label: Two ways to read a probability
sections.body: There are two honest interpretations, and good thinkers switch between them. **Frequency:** over many repeats, how often does it happen? (A coin lands heads ~50% of *many* flips.) **Degree of belief:** how confident am I in this one-off claim? ('70% chance this startup ships on time.') Some events can't be 'repeated' — but you can still assign a probability to your confidence. This second view is what powers Bayes' theorem, coming next lesson.

sections.heading: How to reason with simple probabilities
items: Count the **total** equally-likely outcomes (the sample space).
Count the outcomes that **count as your event**.
Divide: event ÷ total. That's your probability.
For 'A **and** B' of independent events, **multiply** (two coins both heads = ½ × ½ = ¼).
For 'A **or** B' of mutually exclusive events, **add** (rolling a 1 or a 2 = ⅙ + ⅙ = ⅓).

sections.label: Where intuition fails
sections.body: Human brains are terrible at this. We treat a 90% chance as basically certain and then feel 'cheated' by the 10%. We ignore how rare an event is to begin with (the base rate). And we see patterns in pure randomness. Simply *forcing yourself to name a number* — 'I'm about 60% sure' — instantly makes your thinking sharper and more honest than a vague 'probably'.

sections.caption: A clear primer on the basic concepts — sample spaces, events, and computing simple probabilities.

takeaways: A probability is a number from **0 to 1**: favorable outcomes ÷ total equally-likely outcomes.
Two valid readings: long-run **frequency**, and **degree of belief** in a one-off claim.
Combine independent events with **multiply** (and) and mutually-exclusive ones with **add** (or).
Human intuition is bad at odds — we over-trust high probabilities and ignore base rates.
Naming an actual number ('~60% sure') beats vague words and sets up Bayesian updating next.

quiz.q: You roll one fair six-sided die. What's the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
quiz.explain: 'Greater than 4' means 5 or 6 — that's 2 favorable outcomes out of 6, so 2/6 = 1/3 ≈ 0.33.

quiz.q: You flip a fair coin twice. What's the probability of getting heads BOTH times?
quiz.explain: Independent events combine by multiplying: ½ × ½ = ¼. Two heads in a row happens a quarter of the time.

quiz.q: What does it mean to read a probability as a 'degree of belief'?
options: It's always wrong for real events
A measure of your confidence in a claim, even a one-off that can't be repeated
The number of times you've seen it happen
quiz.explain: Some events can't be repeated, but you can still express how confident you are ('70% sure') — the view that underlies Bayesian reasoning.
